title: The Tobacco Master Settlement: That Time We Got Em
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with the iHeart intro voice filling in as co-host) trace the tobacco industry's history of denying health harms and addictiveness, from the 1964 Surgeon General report through the 1990s state attorney general lawsuits that produced the 1998 Tobacco Master Settlement Agreement. They cover the industry's doubt-creating tactics (the Frank Statement, the Roper proposal, Fred Panzer's 1972 memo), youth marketing and the smoking spike among Gen X, the failed McCain bill and Congress's lobbying, the settlement's payments, teen smoking declines, how states spent the money, and the settlement's model for suing over fast food, social media, and opioids. The episode closes with a listener mail segment praising the show's interlude jingles.
topics: stuff you should know listener mail jingles

segments.title: Opening banter and 1964 Surgeon General report
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as a follow-up to the cigarette history episode and recall the 1964 Surgeon General report and warning labels.

segments.title: Industry playbook of doubt and filters
segments.summary: The cigarette industry responded to health claims by demanding proof, promoting filters, forming the Tobacco Industry Research Committee and its ad, and in 1972 Fred Panzer's memo proposed creating doubt about health harms, including the Roper proposal and alternative explanations like extroversion and a constitutional hypothesis.

segments.title: Suppressed research, product placement and youth smoking surge
segments.summary: The industry suppressed studies on addiction and targeted children through movie product placement such as Marlboro in Superman II and Camel Joe ads. Youth smoking peaked in 1997 among Gen X, and the hosts cite replacement smokers and the mid-1990s price war as causes.

segments.title: Denial of addiction and lawsuit record
segments.summary: The industry publicly denied cigarettes were addictive into the 1990s, and it had never lost or settled some four hundred lawsuits, while lobbying states for tort reform.

segments.title: State attorneys general take on the industry
segments.summary: With Congress doing little, state attorneys general led by Michael Moore of Mississippi organized to sue, using Medicaid cost claims and RICO fraud theories, and the hosts describe racing to release documents before they were sealed.

segments.title: The Insider and the strategy of targeting teens
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film The Insider about whistleblower Jeffrey Wigand and explain why attacking teen marketing and public deception was more effective than attacking adult smoking choice. The settlement talks begin in April 1997 with a 368.5 billion dollar opening offer.

segments.title: Congressional fight over McCain bill and federal protections
segments.summary: The federal portion of the deal would have given FDA regulation and liability protection to companies; the protection stuck. Senator John McCain's bill with higher payments and no protection failed after lobbying and unrelated riders. Separately, a flight attendants' secondhand smoke class action settled for 300 million dollars.

segments.title: State-by-state settlements and the 1998 Master Settlement
segments.summary: After Congress stalled, several states settled individually and required public release of documents. In November 1998 the states and the largest companies reached the Master Settlement Agreement, worth 206 billion dollars over 25 years, with bans on cartoon marketing and creation of the Truth Initiative.

segments.title: Major companies, non-participating makers and smokeless tobacco
segments.summary: The settlement covered Philip Morris, R. J. Reynolds, Brown and Williamson and Liggett. Smaller non-participating manufacturers had to pay per-cigarette fees. Smokeless tobacco was handled separately, and dip companies stopped giving free product to sports teams.

segments.title: Tobacco farmers fund and federal RICO case
segments.summary: The settlement put 5.15 billion dollars into a tobacco grower trust fund. The federal government waived its Medicaid recovery share and later sued the companies under RICO in 1999, winning in 2006 a reduced 10 billion dollar penalty plus corrective statements and document release; the FDA was given regulatory authority in 2009.
topics: National Tobacco Growers Settlement Trust Fund
United States v. Philip Morris RICO case

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Second sponsor break before the discussion of impact.

segments.title: Impact: price hikes, youth smoking drop and smoke-free laws
segments.summary: The settlement led to large cigarette price increases, a sharp drop in youth smoking, and state smoke-free laws beginning with Utah and California in 1998. The hosts note vaping and e-cigarette companies escaped the same rules, and Juul paid 462 million to states in 2023.

segments.title: Problems: perpetual payments, securitization and state spending
segments.summary: The annual payments have no end date. Many states used the money for budget gaps and roads, some sold bonds against future payments, less than three percent went to prevention, and North Carolina spent heavily on tobacco farm modernization. Companies had paid about 175 billion, less than half the promised amount, because of inflation and sales-formula offsets.

segments.title: Legacy: suits against fast food, social media and opioids
segments.summary: The hosts argue the settlement became a blueprint for suing companies over harms from intended product use, including social media, opioids and fast food, noting that the opioid industry promoted pseudo-addiction claims.

segments.title: Listener mail: interlude jingles and Rebecca
segments.summary: A listener named Rebecca writes praising the show's Josh-and-Chuck jokes and the listener-made interlude jingles, and the hosts thank Jerry and listeners who submit them.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts explain how to send listener mail and close with the iHeartRadio credit.
